title: Purpose of the organizing practice
blurb: Explain that the organizing practice defines and establishes who is accountable and who is responsible on a PRINCE2 project.
question: Which practice defines and establishes the project's structure of accountability and responsibilities?

teach.body: Formally: the purpose of the organizing practice is to define and establish the project's structure of accountability and responsibilities, summed up as the 'who'. In plain English: before work starts, everyone should know who answers for what, who does what, and who they report to. Without that, decisions stall and work falls between the cracks.

head: Practice
Purpose in a phrase
rows: What, how, where, when, how much
User requirements and how they are met
teach.caption: Organizing is the practice that owns the 'who'. The plans practice also names who does the work, but its purpose is communication and control.

teach.h: Why a project needs its own 'who'
teach.body: Projects are temporary and cross-functional, often spanning several organizations, locations and part-time people. Normal line management rarely fits. PRINCE2 therefore builds a separate project structure in which the business, user and supplier interests are all represented, so accountability is clear even when people come from different employers.

rows.label: Example
values: PM running the project day to day

teach.caption: PRINCE2 7 shows these as the A and R of its RACI tables. Organizing settles both.

children.label: Products
children.sub: PMT structure, role descriptions, commercial approach

teach.caption: Its technique is organizational design and development (five steps), covered later in this topic.

teach.h: When the 'who' is set and revisited

steps.label: Starting up
steps.sub: Appoint the executive and PM, then the PMT

steps.label: Initiation
steps.sub: PMT structure and role descriptions sit in the PID

steps.label: Stage boundaries
steps.sub: Adapt the structure and roles for the next stage

teach.caption: Organizing is not a one-off chart: the structure is adapted at every stage boundary.

teach.h: Worked scenario: a new flood barrier
teach.body: Kestrel Water's directors commission a flood barrier project and name finance director Priya Nandal as executive. She appoints Owen Clarke, head of network operations, as senior user and the civil engineering contractor's director, Bea Lund, as senior supplier. Project manager Tom Achebe records the agreed structure and role descriptions for the PID. Each person now knows what they answer for and what they do: that is the organizing practice at work.

teach.text: Trap: 'organization' was the 6th edition theme; PRINCE2 7 calls it the organizing practice. And organizing is about accountability and responsibility (the 'who'), not about scheduling work (plans) or tracking it (progress).

items: Purpose: define and establish the project's structure of accountability and responsibilities (the 'who').
Accountable = answers for the result; responsible = does the work.
It sets the interests, levels, roles and the products that record them.
Set up in starting up and initiation, adapted at each stage boundary.

summary: You can now state the purpose of the organizing practice and tell it apart from the other six practices. You can also explain the difference between accountability and responsibility, and when the structure is set and revisited.

A.q: What is the purpose of the organizing practice?
options: To judge whether the project remains desirable, viable and achievable
To establish the structure of accountability and responsibilities
To define the products and the means to deliver them
To compare actual achievements against those planned
A.why: The organizing practice defines and establishes the project's structure of accountability and responsibilities, the 'who' (6.1).

whyNot.0: Judging whether the project is desirable, viable and achievable is the business case practice.
whyNot.2: Defining products and the means to deliver them is the plans practice.
whyNot.3: Comparing actual and planned achievement is the progress practice.

A.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. The organizing practice establishes the project's structure of accountability and responsibilities, often summarized as the [?].
options: why
what
when
who
A.why: Organizing is the 'who' of the project (6.1).

whyNot.1: The 'what' is the products, defined in the plans practice.
whyNot.2: The 'when' is an estimate set out in plans.

A.q: Which is defined by the organizing practice?
options: Who is accountable for the project's success
How much tolerance each stage is given
Which risks need a planned response
What quality criteria each product meets
A.why: Organizing establishes accountability and responsibility, for example that the executive is accountable for the project's success.

whyNot.1: Stage tolerances are set by the project board under the progress practice.
whyNot.2: Planning risk responses is part of the risk practice.
whyNot.3: Quality criteria are set in product descriptions under the quality practice.

B.q:
Which two statements about the organizing practice are correct?
1. It defines who is accountable and who is responsible.
2. It sets the tolerances for each stage.
3. It establishes how the business, user and supplier interests are represented.
4. It records the actual costs of each work package.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: Organizing defines accountability and responsibility (1) and makes sure the three project interests are represented in the project's governance (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: stage tolerances are set by the project board as part of progress control.
whyNot.2: Both are false: tolerances and actual costs belong to the progress practice.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: recording actual costs is progress monitoring.

B.q: Which statement about accountability on a PRINCE2 project is correct?
options: The project manager is accountable for the project's success
The senior user is accountable for the business case
The executive's accountability for success cannot be delegated
Project support is accountable for project assurance
B.why: The executive is the single point of accountability for the project, and this accountability cannot be delegated (6.2.4).

whyNot.0: The project manager runs the project day to day; the executive is accountable for its success.
whyNot.1: The executive owns the business case; the senior user specifies the benefits.
whyNot.3: Board members are accountable for assurance; project support must be kept separate from it.

B.q: The executive decides who will be the senior user and the senior supplier. Which practice is being applied?
options: Plans
Progress
Business case
Organizing
B.why: Appointing people to project roles establishes the structure of accountability and responsibilities, which is the organizing practice.

whyNot.0: Plans define the products and how, when and at what cost they will be delivered.
whyNot.1: Progress monitors actual achievement against plans and controls exceptions.
whyNot.2: The business case practice judges whether the project is desirable, viable and achievable.

C.q: Which process first appoints people to the project management team, and which practice does this apply?
options: Starting up a project; organizing
Initiating a project; organizing
Starting up a project; plans
Directing a project; progress
C.why: Starting up a project includes 'appoint the executive and the project manager' and 'appoint the project management team', which apply the organizing practice.

whyNot.1: Initiation records and refines the structure in the PID, but the appointments are made in starting up.
whyNot.2: The process is right, but making appointments applies organizing, not plans.
whyNot.3: Directing a project is the board's process; appointing the PMT is not progress control.

C.q: Once the project is authorized, where are the organizing decisions about roles held, and when are they revisited?
options: In the project brief; at closure
In the PID; at each stage boundary
In the issue register; at each checkpoint
In the business case; with each highlight report
C.why: The PMT structure and role descriptions are part of the PID, and the structure is adapted at stage boundaries (tab 6.5, manage by stages).

whyNot.0: The project brief is superseded by the PID, and roles are revisited at every stage boundary, not just at closure.
whyNot.2: The issue register records formal issues; checkpoints report work package progress.
whyNot.3: The business case holds the justification; highlight reports update the board on stage status.

C.q: A company plans to run a cross-department project through its usual line managers, with no project board. What does this mainly neglect, and what follows?
options: The plans practice; the products have no descriptions
The progress practice; the tolerances become too wide
The organizing practice; the three interests lack a voice
The risk practice; the threats go unrecorded
C.why: Line structures rarely suit cross-functional work. Organizing creates a project structure, with a board that represents business, user and supplier interests.

whyNot.0: Product descriptions come from the plans and quality practices; the gap here is the governance structure.
whyNot.1: Tolerances are a progress matter; the missing piece is who directs and represents each interest.
whyNot.3: Nothing in the plan stops risks being recorded; the gap is accountability and representation.

reteach.title: A house build without a 'who'
reteach.question: If a family hires builders but nobody agrees who decides, who checks the work and who pays, what goes wrong?

blocks.h: Someone must answer for each thing
blocks.body: A house build works when the family (paying and deciding), the people who will live there (using it) and the builders (doing the work) each know their part. The organizing practice does this for a project: it defines and establishes who is accountable and who is responsible, so decisions are made by the right person.

blocks.text: Organizing is the 'who'. Do not confuse it with plans (what, how, when, how much) or progress (tracking actual against planned).

explain.body: The organizing practice defines and establishes the project's structure of accountability and responsibilities: the 'who'.

test.q: The organizing practice is mainly concerned with which question about the project?
options: Why the project is worthwhile
Who is accountable and responsible
What products will be delivered
How progress compares with plan
test.why: Organizing is the 'who': the structure of accountability and responsibilities.

whyNot.0: Whether the project is worthwhile is the business case.
whyNot.2: Which products will be delivered is the plans practice.
whyNot.3: Comparing progress with plan is the progress practice.

explain.body: Being accountable means answering for the result. Being responsible means carrying out the work. The executive is accountable for success; the project manager is responsible for day-to-day management.

test.q: Which describes being accountable in a PRINCE2 RACI table?
options: Carrying out the work allocated to you
Giving advice before a decision is made
Answering for the outcome of the work
Being told about a decision once made
test.why: Accountable means answering for the outcome; the other options describe responsible, consulted and informed.

whyNot.0: Carrying out the work is being responsible.
whyNot.1: Giving advice beforehand is being consulted.
whyNot.3: Being told afterwards is being informed.

explain.body: Organizing covers the three project interests, the four levels of organization, the roles and the rules for combining them, the work breakdown structure, its technique and its management products.

test.q: Which is part of the organizing practice?
options: The probability-impact grid for risks
The product flow diagram for a plan
The highlight report to the board
The four levels of organization
test.why: The four levels (business layer, directing, managing, delivering) are a key concept of the organizing practice.

whyNot.0: The probability-impact grid is a risk practice tool.
whyNot.1: The product flow diagram is part of product-based planning in the plans practice.
whyNot.2: The highlight report is a progress practice product.

explain.body: People are appointed in starting up a project, the structure and role descriptions are held in the PID, and they are adapted at each stage boundary as the project's needs change.

test.q: When are the project management team structure and role descriptions reviewed and adapted?
options: At each stage boundary
At each team checkpoint
When each issue is logged
After the project has closed
test.why: Organizing applies manage by stages by adapting the PMT structure and role descriptions at stage boundaries (tab 6.5).

whyNot.1: Checkpoints report work package progress to the project manager.
whyNot.2: Logging an issue starts the issues technique, not a review of the structure.
whyNot.3: After closure the project management team has been disbanded.
